questions.stem: Which is the best research question for a chemistry investigation?
options: How does the concentration of hydrochloric acid affect the rate of reaction with calcium carbonate?
Is hydrochloric acid too dangerous a chemical to be used by students in a school chemistry laboratory?
Why do people think that some acids are much more useful than other acids?
What is the most interesting reaction that hydrochloric acid can take part in?
questions.explanation: A good research question names the independent variable (acid concentration) and the dependent variable (reaction rate), so it can be answered by collecting data. Questions about danger, opinion or interest cannot be tested by a controlled experiment.

questions.stem: A student investigates how temperature affects the solubility of potassium nitrate. Which is a testable hypothesis?
options: The solubility of potassium nitrate is an interesting property that students should learn about
If the water temperature increases, the mass of potassium nitrate that dissolves in 100 g of water will increase
Potassium nitrate is a useful compound because it is used in fertilisers and in food preservation
Temperature might have some kind of effect on how potassium nitrate behaves when it is placed in water
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction stating the expected relationship between the independent and dependent variables, here temperature and mass dissolved. A vague statement that temperature 'might have some effect' does not predict a direction that data could confirm or reject.

questions.stem: In an experiment on how the mass of zinc affects the volume of hydrogen produced with acid, the room temperature rises during the lesson. What is the room temperature?
options: The independent variable of the experiment
The dependent variable of the experiment
A controlled variable that the student set deliberately
An extraneous variable that could affect the results
questions.explanation: An extraneous variable is one that is not being investigated but could change the results if not controlled. Here temperature affects gas volume and reaction rate, so it should be kept constant or monitored. The independent variable is the mass of zinc.

questions.stem: A student tests whether acid concentration affects reaction rate, but uses fresh marble chips for low concentrations and old, weathered chips for high concentrations. Why are the conclusions doubtful?
options: Chip condition is a confounding factor that changes along with the independent variable
Chip condition is a random error that repeating the trials would cancel out
Chip condition is the dependent variable, so it should have been measured
Chip condition has no effect at all, because only the acid concentration affects the rate
questions.explanation: Because chip condition changes systematically with the acid concentration, any difference in rate could be caused by either factor. This is a confounding factor, and it reduces validity. Repeating the trials would not remove it, because the same pattern would be repeated.

questions.stem: Why should an investigation include several replicates at each value of the independent variable?
options: To change the independent variable over a wider range of values
To reduce the effect of random error and show how reliable the results are
To remove systematic errors caused by poorly calibrated equipment
To make sure that the results agree with the expected theoretical value
questions.explanation: Replicates allow a mean to be calculated, which reduces the effect of random error, and their spread shows how consistent the results are. Repeating a measurement with the same faulty instrument reproduces the same systematic error.

questions.stem: Which describes a systematic error?
options: An error that shifts every measurement in the same direction by a similar amount
An error that makes measurements scatter unpredictably above and below the true value
A one-off mistake, such as writing down 21.5 instead of 25.1
An error that becomes smaller each time the measurement is repeated
questions.explanation: A systematic error, such as a balance that reads 0.05 g too high, pushes all results the same way. Unpredictable scatter is random error, which repeats and averaging reduce. A transcription slip is a mistake, not a type of error in the measurement itself.

questions.stem: An electronic balance reads 0.12 g with nothing on the pan, and the student does not tare it. What effect does this have?
options: A random error that makes the masses scatter by up to 0.12 g
A systematic error that makes every mass 0.12 g too low
No error, because the balance is digital and so is always accurate
A systematic error that makes every mass 0.12 g too high
questions.explanation: A zero offset adds the same amount to every reading, so all masses are 0.12 g too high: a systematic error that reduces accuracy. It can be fixed by taring or calibrating the balance. A digital display does not guarantee accuracy.

questions.stem: A student repeats a titration five times with a burette that was not rinsed with the titrant, so every titre is diluted slightly. Which statement is correct?
options: The repeats reduce random error, but not this systematic error
The repeats remove this systematic error by averaging
The repeats turn this systematic error into a random error
The repeats reduce this systematic error by a factor of about five
questions.explanation: A procedural fault affects every trial in the same direction, so it is a systematic error and averaging cannot remove it. Repeats reduce only random error. The fix is to change the procedure by rinsing the burette with the titrant.

questions.stem: Readings of a temperature probe fluctuate by ±0.2 °C around a steady value from moment to moment. How is this best described, and how is its effect reduced?
options: Random error; replace the probe with a thermometer of the same resolution
Random error; take several readings and calculate a mean
Systematic error; recalibrate the probe against a standard
Systematic error; take several readings and calculate a mean
questions.explanation: Unpredictable fluctuations above and below a value are random error, and averaging several readings reduces its effect. Recalibrating corrects systematic error such as an offset, but does not remove moment-to-moment scatter.

questions.stem: A pipette is labelled 25.00 ± 0.03 mL. What is its percentage uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty ÷ measurement × 100% = 0.03 ÷ 25.00 × 100% = 0.12%. The value 0.03 is the absolute uncertainty, which has units of mL, not a percentage.

questions.stem: Four titres are 20.10, 20.15, 20.05 and 20.10 mL. How should the mean titre be reported with its absolute uncertainty?
questions.explanation: The mean is 80.40 ÷ 4 = 20.10 mL. The absolute uncertainty of the mean is (xmax − xmin) ÷ 2 = (20.15 − 20.05) ÷ 2 = 0.05 mL. Using the full range of 0.10 mL without halving it overstates the uncertainty.

questions.stem: Masses of 1.52, 1.48, 1.50 and 1.54 g are recorded for a precipitate. What is the percentage uncertainty of the mean mass?
questions.explanation: Mean = 6.04 ÷ 4 = 1.51 g. Absolute uncertainty = (1.54 − 1.48) ÷ 2 = 0.03 g. Percentage uncertainty = 0.03 ÷ 1.51 × 100% = 2.0%. Using the full range of 0.06 g gives 4.0%.

questions.stem: How many significant figures are there in 0.00340 g?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are not significant, but the trailing zero after the 4 is significant because it shows the precision of the measurement. The significant figures are 3, 4 and 0.

questions.stem: A student adds masses of 12.52 g and 3.1 g. How should the total be reported?
questions.explanation: When adding or subtracting, the answer keeps the least number of decimal places in the data. The value 3.1 g has one decimal place, so 15.62 rounds to 15.6 g.

questions.stem: A student multiplies 4.56 by 1.4 when processing data. How should the answer be reported?
questions.explanation: When multiplying or dividing, the answer keeps the least number of significant figures in the data. The value 1.4 has two significant figures, so 6.384 is rounded to 6.4.

questions.stem: A burette's initial reading is 0.50 ± 0.02 mL and its final reading is 23.40 ± 0.02 mL. What is the titre with its uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Titre = 23.40 − 0.50 = 22.90 mL. When quantities are added or subtracted, their absolute uncertainties are added, so the uncertainty is 0.02 + 0.02 = 0.04 mL. Uncertainties never cancel when values are subtracted.

questions.stem: In calculating c = n ÷ V, the amount n has a percentage uncertainty of 2.0% and the volume V has 0.5%. What is the percentage uncertainty in c?
questions.explanation: For multiplication and division, percentage uncertainties are added: 2.0% + 0.5% = 2.5%. They are not subtracted even though the operation is division.

questions.stem: The edge of a cubic crystal is measured with a percentage uncertainty of 1.0%. What is the percentage uncertainty in its calculated volume?
questions.explanation: Volume = edge³. For a power, the percentage uncertainty is multiplied by the power, because it is the same as multiplying the measurement by itself three times and adding the percentage uncertainties: 3 × 1.0% = 3.0%.

questions.stem: A student's experimental concentration is 0.095 mol L⁻¹, and the accepted value is 0.100 mol L⁻¹. What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation: Percentage error = |measured − true| ÷ true × 100% = 0.005 ÷ 0.100 × 100% = 5.0%. Dividing by the measured value instead of the true value gives 5.3%.

questions.stem: How does percentage error differ from absolute uncertainty?
options: Percentage error applies only to random errors, while absolute uncertainty applies only to systematic errors
Percentage error compares a result with an accepted value; absolute uncertainty gives the range of the measurement itself
Percentage error gives the range of the measurement itself; absolute uncertainty compares a result with an accepted value
They are the same quantity, but percentage error is always expressed in the same units as the result
questions.explanation: Absolute uncertainty, written as ±, expresses how far a measurement could reasonably vary, and it can be found without knowing the true value. Percentage error needs a theoretical or accepted value and measures how far the result is from it, which reflects accuracy.

questions.stem: A thermometer is graduated in 1 °C divisions. How is a reading from it best recorded?
options: To ±0.01 °C, as precisely as possible
With no uncertainty, as the scale is printed
To ±0.5 °C, half of the smallest division
To ±5 °C, five times the smallest division
questions.explanation: For an analogue scale, the uncertainty of a reading is commonly taken as half the smallest division, here ±0.5 °C. Every measurement has some uncertainty, and quoting ±0.01 °C would claim more precision than the instrument has.

questions.stem: A water sample contains 2.5 mg of copper ions in 500 mL. What is the copper concentration in parts per million?
options: 1.25 ppm
5000 ppm
5.0 ppm
questions.explanation: For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 ppm is 1 mg per litre. 2.5 mg in 0.500 L is 5.0 mg L⁻¹, which is 5.0 ppm. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 1.25.

questions.stem: A sodium chloride solution has a concentration of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ (M = 58.44 g mol⁻¹). What is its concentration in g L⁻¹?
options: 584 g L⁻¹
questions.explanation: Concentration in g L⁻¹ = concentration in mol L⁻¹ × molar mass = 0.100 × 58.44 = 5.84 g L⁻¹. Dividing 0.100 by 58.44 gives 0.00171, which has no meaning here.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines precision?
options: Whether other scientists can confirm the conclusion
How closely repeated measurements agree with each other
How close a measurement is to the true value
Whether the method actually tests the research question
questions.explanation: Precision describes the closeness of repeated measurements to each other, regardless of whether they are correct. Closeness to the true value is accuracy, and whether the method tests what it claims to is validity.

questions.stem: Three students each find the mass of a 10.00 g standard four times. Which set of results is precise but not accurate?
questions.explanation: The first set agrees closely, so it is precise, but its values are about 0.2 g above the true mass, so it is inaccurate, probably because of a systematic error. The second set is both precise and accurate; the others are imprecise.

questions.stem: A student's method for measuring the heat of combustion of a fuel loses most of the heat to the air around the can of water. What is most affected?
options: The reliability only, as the results would vary randomly from trial to trial
The precision only, as the thermometer cannot read the temperature changes finely enough
Nothing, as long as the student repeats the experiment at least three times
The validity of the results, as the method does not measure all the heat released
questions.explanation: If the method does not capture the quantity it claims to measure, the results are not valid; here the heat absorbed by the water is much less than the heat released. Repeating a flawed method gives consistent but wrong results, so repeats do not fix it.

questions.stem: Five groups follow the same procedure to find the concentration of an acid and all obtain 0.112 ± 0.001 mol L⁻¹. The true value is 0.100 mol L⁻¹. What do these results show?
options: They are unreliable, because the percentage error is about 12%
They contain only random error, because the uncertainty is very small
They are reliable but inaccurate, suggesting a systematic error in the procedure
They are accurate and valid, because all five groups obtained the very same result
questions.explanation: Agreement between groups shows that the results are reliable and precise, but they are consistently about 12% above the true value, so they are inaccurate. A shared deviation in one direction points to a systematic error in the procedure. Reliability does not guarantee accuracy.

questions.stem: A calibration line for an AAS analysis passes through (0, 0) and (4.0 ppm, absorbance 0.60). A sample has an absorbance of 0.45. What is its concentration?
options: 2.7 ppm
5.3 ppm
3.0 ppm
questions.explanation: The gradient is 0.60 ÷ 4.0 = 0.15 per ppm, so concentration = absorbance ÷ gradient = 0.45 ÷ 0.15 = 3.0 ppm. Multiplying the absorbance by the gradient instead gives 0.068.

questions.stem: On a scatterplot, the steepest reasonable trendline has a gradient of 0.16 and the least steep has a gradient of 0.14. How should the gradient be reported?
questions.explanation: Maximum and minimum trendlines give a range for the gradient. The best value is their mean, (0.16 + 0.14) ÷ 2 = 0.15, and the uncertainty is half the difference, (0.16 − 0.14) ÷ 2 = 0.01.

questions.stem: What does an R² value of 0.99 for a linear trendline on a scatterplot indicate?
options: The line passes through the origin
The data points lie very close to the straight line
The gradient of the trendline is very close to 1
The results are accurate to 99%
questions.explanation: R² measures how well the trendline fits the data; a value close to 1 means the points lie very close to the line. It says nothing about the size of the gradient or about accuracy, since data with a systematic error can still fit a line perfectly.

questions.stem: A student's graph of reaction rate against temperature curves upwards more and more steeply. What should the student do?
options: Draw a straight line through only the first and the last data points
Remove the higher points so the rest fit a straight line
Join each point to the next with straight segments
Draw a smooth best-fit curve, as the relationship is not linear
questions.explanation: When data clearly follow a curve, a smooth best-fit curve shows the relationship, and forcing a straight line misrepresents it. Removing valid data to fit a preferred pattern is poor practice, and joining point to point treats random scatter as real.

questions.stem: A calibration line was made with standards from 0 to 10 ppm. A sample's reading corresponds to 18 ppm on the extended line. Which response is best?
options: Report the reading with no unit, as it lies outside the range
Dilute the sample so that its reading falls within the range of the standards
Report 18 ppm, because a straight line can always be extended
Report 10 ppm, because that is the highest standard that was measured in the series
questions.explanation: Extrapolating beyond the range of the standards assumes the relationship stays linear, which may not be true at higher concentrations. Diluting the sample by a known factor brings it within range, and the result is then multiplied by the dilution factor.

questions.stem: Where would a student find the hazards, safe handling and first aid information for a chemical such as concentrated ammonia?
options: The periodic table
The class logbook
A chemistry textbook glossary
Its safety data sheet (SDS)
questions.explanation: A safety data sheet gives a chemical's hazards, safe handling and storage, protective equipment, spill and disposal procedures and first aid measures. It is the key document for a risk assessment.

questions.stem: After an experiment, a student has a solution containing lead(II) ions. How should it be disposed of?
options: Into a labelled heavy-metal waste container, as directed by the laboratory procedures
Down the sink with plenty of running water to dilute it until it reaches a safe level
Into the general rubbish bin after soaking it up with paper towel
Into the sink after neutralising it with sodium hydroxide solution
questions.explanation: Heavy-metal ions such as lead are toxic and persist in the environment, so they must be collected in labelled waste containers for proper disposal. Dilution does not make them safe, and neutralising does not remove the metal ions.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a standard operating procedure (SOP) in a laboratory?
options: To give the hypothesis that an investigation is designed to test
To set out the agreed steps for a task so that it is done safely and consistently
To record the results and observations made during an experiment
To list the hazards of each chemical used and the first aid needed for each one
questions.explanation: An SOP is a written set of step-by-step instructions for carrying out a routine task, such as using a fume cupboard, the same safe way each time. Results are recorded in a logbook, and chemical hazards are listed on the safety data sheet.

questions.stem: A student finds a website claiming a new fuel additive greatly improves fuel economy. The site is run by the company selling the additive and cites no data. How should the source be evaluated?
options: It is reliable because the company knows its own product better than anyone else
It is valid because the claim agrees with what most car owners would really like to be true
It can be used without checking, because websites must be accurate by law
It may be biased and lacks evidence, so it should be checked against peer-reviewed studies
questions.explanation: A source with a commercial interest in a claim may be biased, and a claim without data cannot be evaluated. It should be compared with independent, peer-reviewed evidence before being accepted.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of peer review before a scientific paper is published?
options: The authors' friends and colleagues confirm that they agree with the conclusions
The journal checks that the results support existing theories
Readers vote on whether the paper is interesting enough to publish
Independent experts check the methods, data and conclusions for quality
questions.explanation: In peer review, independent experts in the field scrutinise a paper's methods, analysis and conclusions before publication, which helps catch errors and unsupported claims. Results that challenge existing theories can still be published if the work is sound.

questions.stem: Why must a student acknowledge sources and use a standard referencing convention in a report?
options: To credit others' work and let readers locate and check the sources
To make the report longer and more impressive to read
To prove that the student's own results are correct
To avoid having to explain all of the chemistry in their own words
questions.explanation: Referencing gives credit to the original authors, avoids plagiarism and allows readers to find and evaluate the evidence. It does not show that the student's own results are correct.
